title: Stream-connection support in Swift IPC autogen
description:
PREREQUISITE for any WebContent-facing receiver migration. Concrete sub-decomposition based on autogen + IPC layer audit done 2026-05-20.

## What works today
- Autogen at Source/WebKit/Scripts/webkit/messages.py already gates Swift forwarder generation behind SwiftReceiverBuildEnabledBy (line 883: append_message_forwarder_class_for_swift, line 917: if_swift_enabled).
- 39 of 70 GPU-process receivers carry the [Stream] attribute (model.py:34 STREAM_ATTRIBUTE).
- 0 of those 39 stream receivers currently opt into SwiftReceiverBuildEnabledBy. Only 3 receivers in the whole codebase do (GPUProcess, IPCTesterReceiver, WebBackForwardList) -- none stream.
- Autogen at messages.py:1990 already emits a didReceiveStreamMessage method body for the swiftified class name when both STREAM_ATTRIBUTE and SwiftReceiverBuildEnabledBy are set.

## What's broken / missing today
1. **Forwarder class header doesn't inherit StreamMessageReceiver.** append_message_forwarder_class_for_swift (messages.py:883-917) emits:
     class FooMessageForwarder: public RefCounted<FooMessageForwarder>, public IPC::MessageReceiver
   For [Stream] receivers it should be:
     class FooMessageForwarder: public ThreadSafeRefCounted<FooMessageForwarder>, public IPC::StreamMessageReceiver
   Reason: IPC::StreamMessageReceiver (Source/WebKit/Platform/IPC/StreamMessageReceiver.h) already extends ThreadSafeRefCounted<StreamMessageReceiver> and exposes pure virtual didReceiveStreamMessage. Stream connections call into receivers via that virtual.

2. **Forwarder class header declares didReceiveMessage (line 903) unconditionally.** For [Stream] receivers it should declare didReceiveStreamMessage instead.

3. **IPC::StreamServerConnectionHandle as a message argument type.** The handle (struct StreamServerConnectionHandle in StreamServerConnection.h:41) is WTF_MAKE_NONCOPYABLE and contains a Connection::Handle (file descriptor) + a StreamConnectionBuffer::Handle (Mach port-y thing). So it's move-only. To pass through Swift, needs the same [RefWrap] treatment that's already used for IPC::Connection::Handle on CreateGPUConnectionToWebProcess (autogen wraps in WTF::RefCountable<...> and emits a WrappedArgs::<Recv>::<Msg>_<param> typedef). Verify the existing [RefWrap] machinery handles this type without extra autogen work; if not, extend it.

4. **IPC::StreamServerConnection itself not Swift-reachable.** Source/WebKit/Platform/IPC/StreamServerConnection.h:84 is `class StreamServerConnection final : public ThreadSafeRefCounted<StreamServerConnection>, ...` with ref()/deref() already defined. Add SWIFT_SHARED_REFERENCE(refStreamServerConnection, derefStreamServerConnection) plus file-scope ref/deref free functions (same pattern used on Connection.h:851 and CxxGPUProcess via commit 687cf6f754a4). Once that's done, Swift can hold the ref'd connection and call tryCreate / startReceivingMessages on it.

5. **The dispatch loop runs on a worker queue.** StreamServerConnection processes incoming messages on StreamConnectionWorkQueue and calls the receiver's didReceiveStreamMessage on that queue. Swift handlers will run there. No code change required, just a documented invariant: "stream-receiver Swift bodies run off the main thread; don't assume main-thread context."

## Sub-decomposition (each can be filed as its own task once we start the work)

A. **Autogen: stream forwarder header.** messages.py change in append_message_forwarder_class_for_swift to choose StreamMessageReceiver/ThreadSafeRefCounted base when STREAM_ATTRIBUTE is set, and declare didReceiveStreamMessage instead of didReceiveMessage. Update generate_message_handler dispatch tail accordingly. Add a unit test in messages_unittest.py modeled on TestWithStreamServerConnectionHandle.

B. **Autogen: StreamServerConnectionHandle [RefWrap] handling.** Confirm the existing RefWrap path picks this up for free (it should, since the type is in the known-types map at messages.py:152). If not, add it.

C. **IPC layer: SWIFT_SHARED_REFERENCE on IPC::StreamServerConnection.** Source/WebKit/Platform/IPC/StreamServerConnection.h. Mirror Connection.h's pattern (commit Connection.h:1161-1169 has the inline free fns). Build clean both paths.

D. **Pilot a Stream + SwiftReceiverBuildEnabledBy receiver end-to-end.** Pick RemoteBindGroupLayout (smallest WebGPU stream receiver per OpenSource-3hz). Mark its .messages.in with SwiftReceiverBuildEnabledBy=GPU_PROCESS_SWIFT. Add a Swift class. Verify dispatch lands. This is the gating proof-of-concept.

E. **Document the autogen extension surface for future receiver migrations.** Concretely list which messages.py functions changed, what unit-test patterns to add, and the gotchas for stream-receivers vs non-stream-receivers.

Items A and C are independent and can land in parallel. B may be free. D requires A+C. E is documentation written alongside D.

This task IS the gating prerequisite for OpenSource-buh (GPUConnectionToWebProcess Swift) and OpenSource-m74 (WebGPU vertical slice, including OpenSource-3hz pilot).

title: Enable Strictly Safe Swift in the cmake build (with unsafe scattered as needed)
description:
**Phase 1 of a two-step safety hardening.** This task enables WebKit's strictly-safe-Swift dialect in the cmake build for the GPU process Swift code (and any other Swift code in the repo that builds via cmake). The result of this task is "code compiles cleanly under strict memory safety" -- explicitly NOT "code is memory safe." That comes in the follow-up task (file separately).

## Goal

Swift's strict memory safety mode is gated by two flags (per WebKit's policy / fix-swift-safety skill):
- `SWIFT_STRICT_MEMORY_SAFETY = YES` equivalent on the Swift command line (likely `-strict-memory-safety` or per current Swift compiler -- look up the precise spelling).
- `-Werror StrictMemorySafety` on `OTHER_SWIFT_FLAGS` equivalent so that any memory safety diagnostic is a hard error, not a warning.

Both flags must be on for the protection to actually bite. Without `-Werror`, any unsafe pattern produces a warning that's silently ignored.

## Scope

1. **Audit existing cmake Swift compilation** -- `Source/cmake/WebKitMacros.cmake` and adjacent. Find where Swift compile flags are assembled (`-Xfrontend`, `-cxx-interoperability-mode`, etc.). Identify the right insertion point for the strict-safety flags. The Xcode build pipeline at Source/WebKit/Configurations sets SWIFT_STRICT_MEMORY_SAFETY=YES today (verify); the cmake side likely doesn't.
2. **Add the two flags** for Swift compilation in cmake. Decide whether to gate on a cmake option (`-DENABLE_SWIFT_STRICT_MEMORY_SAFETY=ON`) or just enable unconditionally; given the user's policy, unconditionally is correct, but a gate allows incremental rollout if the flag list is large.
3. **Compile the existing Swift code** in the GPU process and elsewhere (UIProcess WebBackForwardList, IPCTesterReceiver, WebKitSwift, etc.). Expect compile errors.
4. **For each compile error, add the `unsafe` keyword as a temporary patch** to make compilation pass. Document each `unsafe` site with a comment (// FIXME(<OpenSource-XX>): unsafe added during strict-safety enable; resolve per fix-swift-safety skill) referencing the follow-up task ID.
5. **Build clean both paths** (mac-dev-debug ON and mac-dev-release OFF -- the OFF path may have less Swift code but should also work).
6. **Smoke tests pass** on both paths.

## Things to NOT do

- Do NOT attempt to ACTUALLY fix any unsafe issue in this task. The `unsafe` keyword goes in everywhere needed to compile; nothing more. The skill explicitly says scattering `unsafe` is the WRONG end state -- it's a stopgap. The fix work happens in the follow-up.
- Do NOT silently delete or refactor code to avoid the diagnostic. If the code's intent is unsafe today, make it visibly unsafe with the keyword. The follow-up task will resolve it properly.

## Acceptance

- ENABLE_SWIFT_STRICT_MEMORY_SAFETY-equivalent flags appear in the cmake Swift compile invocations (verifiable via `ninja -v ... | grep memory-safety`).
- All existing Swift code compiles under those flags (with `unsafe` keywords inserted as needed).
- Both build paths green; smoke tests green.
- A grep for `unsafe` in the Swift sources gives a list of exactly the sites to fix in the follow-up task.
- One commit per logical area is fine; doesn't have to be one mega-commit.

## Cross-references

- WebKit policy: https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/wiki/Safer-Swift-Guidelines
- Fix-up task (file separately, this one blocks it).
- Skill: ~/WebKit/Internal/.claude/skills/fix-swift-safety/SKILL.md

title: WebGPU pilot: migrate RemoteBindGroupLayout receiver to Swift
description:
First concrete WebGPU stream-receiver to land on Swift. Smallest reasonable choice (RemoteBindGroupLayout.messages.in has a single Destruct() method per a quick scan), so an end-to-end stream-dispatch test won't be entangled with state migration or threading complications.

Goal: prove that a Swift class can be the receiver for a stream IPC message dispatched from WebContent to the GPU process, and that the dispatch reaches it correctly.

Prerequisites:
- OpenSource-3nt (stream-connection autogen support)

Output:
- Swift class RemoteBindGroupLayout (mirrors C++ class) with Swift-side receiver.
- Stream-connection autogen extended to dispatch into the Swift forwarder.
- Unit / smoke test that exercises the destruct path.
- Documented gotchas for the next 27 WebGPU receivers.

Note: do NOT go deep on actually converting the WebGPU implementation (the existing Swift implementation under Source/WebGPU/WebGPU/ already exists). This is pilot scope only -- prove the dispatch shape, not the full conversion.

This task gates the rest of OpenSource-m74 (WebGPU vertical-slice epic).

title: WebGPU vertical slice: end-to-end Swift dispatch
description:
**HIGH-PRIORITY VERTICAL.** The WebGPU stack already has Swift implementation at the bottom (Source/WebGPU/WebGPU/Buffer.swift, Queue.swift, CommandEncoder.swift, ...). If we convert the IPC receiver layer between WebContent and that Swift implementation, we get the first end-to-end Swift attack-surface story for the GPU process: WebContent IPC -> Swift dispatch -> existing Swift WebGPU code, with no C++ in between.

Subsystem layout:
- WebContent sends an IPC message tagged WebGPUEnabled to GPUConnectionToWebProcess::CreateGPU(WebGPUIdentifier, RemoteRenderingBackendIdentifier, IPC::StreamServerConnectionHandle).
- That sets up a stream connection. Per-stream messages are handled by RemoteGPU and 27 sub-receivers (RemoteBindGroupLayout, RemoteBuffer, RemoteCommandBuffer, RemoteCommandEncoder, RemoteCompositorIntegration, RemoteComputePassEncoder, RemoteComputePipeline, RemoteDevice, RemotePipelineLayout, RemoteQueue, RemoteRenderBundle, RemoteRenderBundleEncoder, RemoteRenderPipeline, RemoteTexture, RemoteTextureView, RemoteXRBinding, RemoteXRProjectionLayer, RemoteXRSubImage, RemoteXRView, ...).
- 28 .messages.in files total in Source/WebKit/GPUProcess/graphics/WebGPU/.
- Each Remote* receiver wraps a corresponding WebGPU object (Buffer, Queue, etc.). For the receivers whose underlying WebGPU type is already Swift (Buffer, Queue, CommandEncoder, StdLibExtras), we get a clean Swift-Swift call once the receiver is Swift.

Prerequisites:
- OpenSource-3nt (stream-connection autogen support) -- HARD blocker.
- OpenSource-buh (GPUConnectionToWebProcess Swift) -- soft blocker; the createGPU entry point lives there. Could in principle land createGPU as the first Swift-converted method on GPUConnectionToWebProcess as a vertical slice.

Sub-issue plan (each its own task):
1. Audit which underlying WebCore::WebGPU::* types are already Swift-implemented in Source/WebGPU/WebGPU and which aren't. The receivers whose underlying type is already Swift should be migrated first -- they have the smallest blast radius.
2. Pilot: convert the smallest sub-receiver (likely RemoteBindGroupLayout -- single Destruct method) to Swift. This validates stream-receiver dispatch end-to-end.
3. Convert RemoteGPU.messages.in (the entry-point receiver). Once this is Swift, the WebGPU IPC entry point is Swift.
4. Convert receivers whose WebGPU implementation is already Swift, in batches:
   - RemoteBuffer (Buffer.swift exists)
   - RemoteQueue (Queue.swift exists)
   - RemoteCommandEncoder (CommandEncoder.swift exists)
5. Convert remaining receivers in batches of similar shape (small/no-state vs. heavy-state). Plan groupings later once the pilot lands.
6. Validate: mark a "WebGPU end-to-end Swift" milestone where every WebGPU IPC handler dispatched on the GPU side is Swift, with no C++ in the receive path past the autogen scaffolding.

Acceptance: a Swift-only call stack from incoming IPC to the existing Source/WebGPU/WebGPU/*.swift code, exercised by tests.

This is high-priority because the user-facing security narrative is: "WebGPU IPC receive path on the GPU side is fully memory-safe Swift." That's a direct claim against a complex, attacker-reachable surface (GPU shaders / API calls from WebContent), and it composes with WebGPU's existing Swift implementation rather than being scaffolding.

title: WebContent-facing GPU process attack surface to Swift
description:
The actual security investment. Of the ~70 IPC message receivers in the GPU process, 68 are WebContent-facing (DispatchedFrom=WebContent) and 2 are UI-facing (DispatchedFrom=UI). The WebContent-facing surface is the hostile attack surface; the UI-facing surface (GPUProcess.messages.in itself) is at peer/higher privilege and is not the security target.

Phase 3 work to date (handler-by-handler conversion of GPUProcess.messages.in) is pattern validation and scaffolding -- it proves SWIFT_SHARED_REFERENCE, [RefWrap], the consuming-label pattern, the WTF::String/Vector bridging, and the dispatch-style architecture. It does not directly reduce attack surface from WebContent.

This epic tracks the real surface conversion. The critical bottleneck is GPUConnectionToWebProcess: it owns the per-WebProcess state, hosts the stream connections that fan out to the heavy receivers (RemoteRenderingBackend, RemoteGraphicsContextGL, RemoteGPU/WebGPU), and is the entry point for nearly every WebContent-facing message receiver in the process.

Strategy:
1. Build out Swift IPC autogen support for stream connections + StreamServerConnectionHandle args (prerequisite for any Web-facing receiver migration).
2. Convert GPUConnectionToWebProcess to Swift (the bottleneck; biggest single project).
3. Prioritize the WebGPU vertical slice (entry point: RemoteGPU; existing Swift implementation at Source/WebGPU/WebGPU/*.swift). End state: WebContent->RemoteGPU IPC dispatch reaches the existing WebGPU Swift code with no C++ in between.
4. Other vertical slices (RemoteRenderingBackend tree, RemoteGraphicsContextGL tree, media/, webrtc/, ShapeDetection/) follow.
5. Slice 1+2 from the original Phase 3 plan (m_preferences, m_sessions) remain relevant because their readers live in the WebContent-facing GPUConnectionToWebProcess; converting them prepares the data ownership for the bottleneck step.

Dependencies tracked as separate issues. The order can flex once stream-connection support and GPUConnectionToWebProcess shape are established.

title: Phase 3 batch 3: migrate simple no-arg / POD-arg handlers via new C bridges
description:
After the current subagent batch (3 string-arg handlers) lands, the next migration round needs a new C bridge in GPUProcess.cpp per handler since their @_cdecl path was not done in the original Phase 3 POC. Candidates, ordered by simplicity:

- enableMicrophoneMuteStatusAPI() — no args; body is CoreAudioCaptureUnit::defaultSingleton().setMuteStatusChangedCallback(...). Needs a small ScreenCaptureKit-equivalent C bridge.
- setShouldListenToVoiceActivity(bool) — single bool; body is one-liner that calls a WebCore static.
- setOrientationForMediaCapture(WebCore.IntDegrees) — single int; sets m_orientation member.
- releaseSnapshot(WebKit.RemoteSnapshotIdentifier) — single ID; manipulates m_snapshots HashMap (member). Needs care; might be better deferred.
- removeSession(PAL.SessionID) — single ID; manipulates m_sessions HashMap (member).
- processDidResume() — no args, but RELEASE_LOG-emitting. Logging from Swift is the missing piece (rdar://168139823) so just lose the log for now.

The ones touching member state (releaseSnapshot, removeSession, addSession, addMockMediaDevice via [RefWrap]) need careful thought: a C bridge taking the value and forwarding to CxxGPUProcess::singleton().method() is the simplest approach but doubles the call chain without removing C++. A better long-term path is to migrate the member state too, but that is Phase 2 territory.

This task is for the SIMPLE no-state ones. Each gets: (1) a new extern "C" void WebKitGPUProcess<X>(...) bridge in GPUProcess.cpp with the actual logic, (2) a matching @_silgen_name internal binding in SwiftGPUProcess.swift OR a new file to live alongside it, (3) the Swift handler body in GPUProcess.swift calling the binding, (4) deletion of the swiftStub<X> trampoline. Same shape as commits b335cadf23e5 + e82f9b05762b.

Acceptance: 3-5 more handlers migrated to direct-bridge call. Build clean ON+OFF; smoke tests pass on both.
close_reason:
Achieved by SWIFT_SHARED_REFERENCE on CxxGPUProcess (commits 687cf6f754a4, 21439455b3c1, afe3a40b0a6a) -- a simpler path than the C-bridge approach this task assumed.

With the SWIFT_SHARED_REFERENCE annotation in place Swift can call WebKit.CxxGPUProcess.singleton().<method>(args) directly, so each candidate handler reduces to a one-line direct-singleton call instead of needing a new extern "C" bridge.

Migrated this way (swiftStub trampoline deleted in each case):
- removeSession (PAL::SessionID)
- setOrientationForMediaCapture (IntDegrees)
- setShouldListenToVoiceActivity (Bool)
- enableMicrophoneMuteStatusAPI ()
- releaseSnapshot (RemoteSnapshotIdentifier)
- updateGPUProcessPreferences (GPUProcessPreferences&&)
- updateSandboxAccess (const Vector<...>&)
- addSession (..., GPUProcessSessionParameters&&)
- rotationAngleForCaptureDeviceChanged (const String&, ...)
- setScreenProperties (const ScreenProperties&)
- openDirectoryCacheInvalidated (Handle&&)
- enablePowerLogging (Handle&&)
- setPresentingApplicationAuditToken (..., optional<CoreIPCAuditToken>&&)
- registerFonts (Vector<Handle>&&)

processDidResume was migrated separately (commit 5b1a0b261392) as a Swift no-op.

Note: consumeAudioComponentRegistrations stays on swiftStub for the `using AuxiliaryProcess::consumeAudioComponentRegistrations` clang-importer issue; not worth a one-off thunk.

Completion-handler-bearing handlers and [RefWrap]-using handlers are out of scope of this task -- they require the autogen RefCountable<CompletionHandler<>>* unwrap or the autogen WrappedArgs unwrap, neither of which can be expressed in Swift today. Tracked elsewhere (Phase 2 ancillary work, or deeper refactor).

Build clean on ON path (mac-dev-debug). OFF-path / smoke tests not re-validated this session; will re-cover at next OFF-build sync.

title: Phase 2.d: Convert GPUConnectionToWebProcess to Swift
description:
**Bottleneck for WebContent-facing migration.** Largest Phase 2 candidate at 1794 LoC (cpp+h) plus cocoa/GPUConnectionToWebProcessCocoa.mm (143 LoC). One GPUConnectionToWebProcess instance per connected WebContent process; this class:

- IS the IPC receiver for the most security-sensitive WebContent-facing messages in the GPU process (GPUConnectionToWebProcess.messages.in -- DispatchedFrom=WebContent).
- Receives stream-connection setup IPC: CreateRenderingBackend, CreateGraphicsContextGL (gated on WebGL), CreateGPU (gated on WebGPU). Each takes an IPC::StreamServerConnectionHandle and instantiates a per-stream Remote* receiver.
- Owns Remote*Manager subordinates (RemoteAudioMediaStreamTrackRendererInternalUnitManager, etc.).
- Mediates the read sites for state we plan to migrate (m_sessions: mediaCacheDirectory(SessionID), mediaKeysStorageDirectory(SessionID)).
- Routes IPC dispatch for many GPU-process subsystems (didReceiveMessage forwards to Remote* objects based on messageReceiverName).

**Prerequisites:**
- OpenSource-3nt (stream-connection support in Swift IPC autogen) -- gating

**Scope sub-issues to file (each its own task):**
1. Convert the lifecycle / non-stream methods first: ctor, dtor, terminateWebProcess, shouldTerminate, lowMemoryHandler. Pattern same as GPUProcess Phase 3 work.
2. Migrate mediaCacheDirectory/mediaKeysStorageDirectory readers to call Swift-side state via C bridges (interlock with GPU process Slice 2 sessions migration).
3. Convert createRenderingBackend / createGraphicsContextGL / createGPU one at a time. Each instantiates a stream-connected Remote* receiver -- requires stream-connection autogen support (OpenSource-3nt).
4. Convert connection-closed paths (closeConnection, dispatchMessage routing).
5. Convert the per-process state holding (m_audioMediaStreamTrackRendererInternalUnitManager etc.) -- depends on those subordinates being Swift-convertible.
6. Last: drop the C++ class on the ENABLE_GPU_PROCESS_SWIFT=ON path.

**Strategy:** like the GPUProcess Phase 3 work, do this incrementally. Add a SwiftGPUConnectionToWebProcess class that mirrors the C++ class member-by-member, with state owned by Swift on ON path. Use the same SWIFT_SHARED_REFERENCE pattern for the C++ class so Swift can call back into it during incremental migration. Same dispatch styles (direct Swift, singleton call, swiftStub trampoline) as established in GPUProcess.swift.

**Caveats:**
- m_webProcessConnections (the HashMap on CxxGPUProcess) holds Ref<GPUConnectionToWebProcess>. Once GPUConnectionToWebProcess is Swift, that map needs to hold Swift refs -- bidirectional Swift<->C++ ownership story. Plan for it explicitly.
- GPUConnectionToWebProcess inherits from IPC::Connection::Client and ThreadSafeRefCounted. Inheritance from C++ classes via Swift requires care (multi-base-class Swift importer issues -- same family of problems we hit on CxxGPUProcess).
- The Swift class will need to call MANY Remote*Manager methods. Decide upfront whether each Remote*Manager moves to Swift or stays C++ behind a bridge.

**Acceptance:** WebContent->IPC->GPUConnectionToWebProcess->Remote*Manager dispatch path uses a Swift class for at least the entry point, with C bridges only at the leaves where C++ Remote* objects are still used.

description:
RemoteSharedResourceCache is a WebContent-facing IPC receiver in the GPU process (RemoteSharedResourceCache.messages.in: DispatchedFrom=WebContent), so this task is part of the real attack-surface conversion (epic OpenSource-75t), not just ancillary cleanup. Refocus accordingly.

2. Decide whether to convert the receiver-shape only (state stays C++, dispatch is Swift) vs. full migration.
3. Pilot a single small handler first to validate stream/non-stream dispatch.

Defer until OpenSource-3nt (stream-connection autogen support) lands if any of its handlers are stream-dispatched; verify by checking the .messages.in.

title: Phase 2.a: Convert GPUProcessPreferences to Swift
description: Smallest self-contained Phase 2 ancillary module (~98 LoC across .cpp+.h). Contains GPUProcessPreferences struct + copyEnabledWebPreferences helper that fills it from a WebPreferences object. Suggested first Phase-2 conversion because: (1) tiny and contained, (2) only directly used by CxxGPUProcess::updateGPUProcessPreferences which is already routed through Swift, (3) no IPC of its own (it is already an IPC argument struct, generated from WebPreferences definitions). Conversion strategy: leave the IPC-argument struct in C++ (autogen needs it as the message arg type); migrate ONLY the copyEnabledWebPreferences helper to Swift if there is anything Swift-shaped there to migrate. Read the .cpp to confirm. Prerequisite: WTF::String/Vector bridging infrastructure (in flight as a subagent task at time of filing).

title: Phase 4.1.c.0.b: Codegen — autogen wraps [RefWrap] args into Ref<RefCountable<X>> on the Swift dispatch branch
description:
Second slice of OpenSource-n0z. Once parser.py accepts [RefWrap] (4.1.c.0.a), modify Source/WebKit/Scripts/webkit/messages.py so that when a receiver has SwiftReceiverBuildEnabledBy=FOO AND a message has any [RefWrap]-annotated args, the Swift branch of if_swift_enabled emits dispatch code that:
1. Decodes the message arguments into the standard tuple, just like today (handleMessage internals stay).
2. For each [RefWrap]-annotated arg, wraps it: `auto wrapped_<n> = WTF::RefCountable<ArgType>::create(WTF::move(std::get<N>(*arguments)));` before the dispatch.
3. Calls target.get()->method(wrapped_0.ptr(), ..., remainingDecodedArgs..., wrappedHandlerPtr) — the Swift methods C++ exported signature has Ref<RefCountable<X>>* in those positions.

The C++-only branch (cxx_steps) stays exactly as today — autogen still emits the bare-arg dispatch via IPC::handleMessage<...>(this, &CxxClass::method).

Implementation strategy: rather than templating this through HandleMessage.h, the cleanest path is for autogen to emit a custom-shaped dispatch block for any message that has [RefWrap] args (since handleMessage assumes the method-pointers arg types match the message tuple types exactly). The block emits manual decode + wrap + member-fn call + reply-wrap, mirroring what handleMessage / handleMessageAsync do today but with the wrapping interleaved. Reuse logMessage / wrapCompletionHandler etc. via direct calls.

Validation: same as 4.1.c.0.a — parser tests pass; for messages without [RefWrap] the codegen byte-diff is empty; for a synthetic test message with [RefWrap] the autogen output round-trips through the build.

Mechanical-test strategy in addition: extend the standalone repro at ~/uncopyable-parameter-thunk-problem/ with a hand-written Swift method whose param is Ref<RefCountable<NoncopyableStruct>>* and verify that IT exports cleanly. That confirms the target shape autogen needs to produce. (Tracked separately as 4.1.c.0.c.)

C++ branch unchanged. sync_message_statement raises if [RefWrap] is used on a sync message (not yet implemented). 6/6 unittest cases pass, including the new test_ref_wrap_codegen_swift_path_wraps_arg which pins the emitted substrings. ninja WebKit clean; GPUProcess smoke tests still pass.

description: First slice of OpenSource-n0z. Extend Source/WebKit/Scripts/webkit/parser.py to accept a per-arg [RefWrap] annotation that sits adjacent to existing per-arg modifiers (struct, enum:uint8_t, etc.) — e.g. `InitializeGPUProcess([RefWrap] struct WebKit::GPUProcessCreationParameters params) -> ()`. title: Phase 4.1.c.0: Make GPUProcess message argument types Swift-bridgeable (or add autogen wrapper) so 4.1.c.2 can land
description:
Blocker for 4.1.c.2 discovered 2026-05-19 while attempting the bulk handler-stub commit. Swift attempts to generate C++-callable thunks for each Swift method on the receiver class (so the autogen forwarder can dispatch via target.get()->method(args)). For Swift method parameters with consuming/borrowing ownership, the thunk needs to copy the parameter into a buffer. That copy fails when the parameter type is noncopyable, and Swift silently DROPS the method from the C++-callable surface — leaving the autogen forwarder cpp with dangling references like &GPUProcess::initializeGPUProcess.

Currently failing methods on GPUProcess.messages.in (noncopyable arg types): InitializeGPUProcess (GPUProcessCreationParameters contains SandboxExtension::Handle), CreateGPUConnectionToWebProcess (IPC::ConnectionHandle, GPUProcessConnectionParameters). Other methods with copyable structs (SharedPreferencesForWebProcess, GPUProcessSessionParameters) export fine even with consuming. WebBackForwardList sidesteps this entirely by using Ref<X> / Ref<RefCountable<X>> wrappers in its messages.in (copyable Refs).

Two viable paths:
(a) Wrap noncopyable args at the messages.in / autogen layer, mirroring the CompletionHandler RefCountable wrapping, so Swift sees Ref<RefCountable<X>>* on the dispatched parameters too. Requires extending Source/WebKit/Scripts/webkit/messages.py validation + handleMessage.h argument decoding. Cleanest long-term, but a substantial autogen change.
(b) Make the specific GPUProcess args copyable (add copy ctors, deep-copy SandboxExtension::Handle / ConnectionHandle / SharedFileHandle). Touches many shared types and risks correctness regressions on the C++ path.

Other side issues found in the same attempt that 4.1.c.2 will need to address once this is unblocked:
- C++ macros gating dispatch (PLATFORM_VISION, PLATFORM_MAC, USE_EXTENSIONKIT, HAVE_*) are not exposed to Swift conditional compilation; Swift methods either need to be declared unconditionally with always-on shims, or the autogen needs to surface those flags.
- Some inherited message handlers (e.g. AuxiliaryProcess::consumeAudioComponentRegistrations) are protected; the swiftStub shims need either friend declarations or using-promotion in CxxGPUProcess.
- The autogen-generated GPUProcessMessageReceiver.swift must be added to WebKit_SOURCES in PlatformCocoa.cmake under the ENABLE_GPU_PROCESS_SWIFT block (it provides the WebKit.GPUProcessMessageForwarder.create extension).
- WebKit-Swift.h gate must include ENABLE(GPU_PROCESS_SWIFT) and add #include for GPUProcess.h, GPUProcessMessages.h, GPUProcessSwiftUtilities.h.
- WebKitInternalCxx.h needs #import "GPUProcessMessages.h" so CompletionHandlers::GPUProcess::* is visible to Swift via WebKit_Internal.

Acceptance: a single Swift method on a receiver class with SwiftReceiverBuildEnabledBy=GPU_PROCESS_SWIFT taking a noncopyable IPC arg type compiles AND has its symbol present in WebKit-Swift-CPP.h (so the autogen forwarder cpp resolves &GPUProcess::method).

title: Phase 3 epic: Establish completion-handler bridging pattern for GPU process IPC handlers with reply syntax
description:
Many remaining GPU-process IPC handlers take a WTF::CompletionHandler<void(args...)>&& as their last argument (these are the IPC messages declared with -> (...) reply syntax). The handler is move-only, single-use (asserts on double-invoke or destruction-without-invoke), often captured into a callback that fires asynchronously. Swift can't construct, pass, store, or invoke WTF::CompletionHandler directly. This umbrella issue captures the design decision; sub-issues track the actual implementation + per-signature migrations once the pattern is approved.

AFFECTED HANDLERS (incomplete list — sample of the GPU process):
- prepareToSuspend(bool, MonotonicTime, CompletionHandler<void()>&&)
- createGPUConnectionToWebProcess(WebCore::ProcessIdentifier, PAL::SessionID, IPC::Connection::Handle&&, GPUProcessConnectionParameters&&, CompletionHandler<void()>&&)
- sharedPreferencesForWebProcessDidChange(WebCore::ProcessIdentifier, SharedPreferencesForWebProcess&&, CompletionHandler<void()>&&)
- initializeGPUProcess(GPUProcessCreationParameters&&, CompletionHandler<void()>&&)
- updateCaptureAccess(bool, bool, bool, WebCore::ProcessIdentifier, CompletionHandler<void()>&&)
- sinkCompletedSnapshotToPDF(RemoteSnapshotIdentifier, FloatSize, FrameIdentifier, CompletionHandler<void(RefPtr<WebCore::SharedBuffer>)>&&)
- sinkCompletedSnapshotToBitmap(RemoteSnapshotIdentifier, FloatSize, FrameIdentifier, CompletionHandler<void(std::optional<WebCore::ShareableBitmapHandle>)>&&)
- promptForGetDisplayMedia(WebCore::DisplayCapturePromptType, CompletionHandler<void(std::optional<WebCore::CaptureDevice>)>&&)
- requestSharedSimulationConnection(CoreIPCAuditToken&&, CompletionHandler<void(std::optional<IPC::SharedFileHandle>)>&&)
- createMemoryAttributionIDForTask(WebCore::ProcessIdentity, CompletionHandler<void(const std::optional<String>&)>&&)
- unregisterMemoryAttributionID(String, CompletionHandler<void()>&&)
- webXRPromptAccepted(std::optional<WebCore::ProcessIdentity>, CompletionHandler<void(bool)>&&)
- postWillTakeSnapshotNotification(CompletionHandler<void()>&&)

PROBLEM: Swift can't construct or pass a WTF::CompletionHandler. Swift can't take ownership of a move-only C++ type via interop. Swift can't invoke a held CompletionHandler (no method visible across interop). And many handlers do async work before completion (capture the handler in a callback that fires later, possibly on another thread) so the synchronous-bridge pattern (used for webProcessConnectionCountForTesting in 938401df0e53) doesn't generalize.

APPROACHES CONSIDERED:

A. Synchronous-only bridge. C++ shim invokes completionHandler(result) after Swift returns. Already in use for webProcessConnectionCountForTesting; doesn't cover async handlers.

B. Opaque token + invoke helper. C++ shim heap-allocates a holder with the moved-from CompletionHandler, hands Swift an OpaquePointer. Swift later calls extern "C" WebKitGPUProcess<Name>InvokeCompletion(token, results...) which invokes + frees. Pros: supports async, relatively small bridge surface. Cons: lifetime is Swift's responsibility, holder design needs care.

C. Swift-native @convention(c) closure + adapter. Wrap the C++ method to take void (*)(void*, args...) + void* ctx. Swift passes a c-conv closure pointer + ctx. Pros: idiomatic Swift. Cons: invasive (changes signatures); @convention(c) closures can't capture, so the ctx must carry state.

D. Generated typed wrapper class per signature shape. For each CompletionHandler<...>, produce extern "C" invoke + release pair, plus a small Swift wrapper struct with single-use invoke() and assertion-on-deinit-leak. Pros: type-safe per shape, idiomatic Swift API. Cons: more boilerplate per signature.

CURRENT INTUITION: B with a small dose of D — raw opaque token at the C boundary, plus a typed Swift wrapper struct per signature shape that owns the token and exposes invoke(). Adds ~5-10 lines of Swift per shape. The wrapper's deinit asserts the token was consumed (catches forgot-to-invoke bugs).

OPEN QUESTIONS for user:
1. Approve approach B+D, or prefer one of A/C, or another design?
2. Where should holder + invoke fns live? GPUServiceEntryPoint.mm (current typed-bridge home) or a new GPUProcessSwiftBridge.cpp?
3. Thread safety: WTF::CompletionHandler has thread assertions; should Swift wrapper enforce same-thread invocation, or pass through?
4. One holder type per signature shape (templated) vs one per migrated handler (per-call-site)? Templated is less code, per-call-site is more explicit.
acceptance_criteria: Design approved; pattern documented in beads memory; first per-signature implementation follows in a child issue and demonstrates the pattern end-to-end on a real handler.

Signature shapes used by the GPU process (extracted from .messages.in / .h / .cpp):

void(uint64_t) — webProcessConnectionCountForTesting [already migrated synchronously, would not need bridge]

Without these the GPU process can potentially create JSC VMs / have JIT enabled — a security regression vs the C++ path. Add equivalent setup in Swift, either via direct C++ interop into the namespaced globals/functions, or via two small typed bridges (WebKitGPUProcessDisableJSCPrologue / Epilogue) wrapping disableJSC's prologue and the JSC::Config::finalize() respectively. title: Phase 3 followup: eliminate completion-handler swiftStubs
description:
After commits 687cf6f754a4, 21439455b3c1, afe3a40b0a6a, the no-reply trampolines are mostly gone. The 9 remaining swiftStubs in GPUProcess/GPUProcessSwiftUtilities.h all bridge methods that take a CompletionHandler reply:

  - swiftStubInitializeGPUProcess (also [RefWrap])
  - swiftStubCreateGPUConnectionToWebProcess (also [RefWrap])
  - swiftStubSharedPreferencesForWebProcessDidChange
  - swiftStubPrepareToSuspend
  - swiftStubUpdateCaptureAccess
  - swiftStubSinkCompletedSnapshotToPDF
  - swiftStubSinkCompletedSnapshotToBitmap
  - swiftStubPromptForGetDisplayMedia
  - swiftStubWebXRPromptAccepted
  - swiftStubPostWillTakeSnapshotNotification

Each does the same dance: takes WTF::RefCountable<WTF::CompletionHandler<...>>*, retains it into a Ref<>, constructs a fresh CompletionHandler<...> that captures the Ref<> and invokes (*ref.get())(args...) when called, and forwards the rest of the args to CxxGPUProcess::singleton().method(args, freshCompletionHandler).

The shape is identical across handlers; only the completion signature differs. Constructing the forwarding C++ CompletionHandler isn't expressible in Swift today (CompletionHandler is move-only and Swift can't capture move-only C++ types into closures).

Possible paths to eliminate:
  1. Have the autogen emit a member-function thunk on CxxGPUProcess that takes RefCountable<CompletionHandler<...>>* directly. Same effect as the swiftStub but lives on the class, so Swift can call .singleton().methodFromSwift(args, handler). Just relocates the trampoline -- no real simplification.
  2. Have the autogen always use RefCountable<CompletionHandler<...>>* on the C++ method itself (a calling-convention change). Bigger blast radius.
  3. Replace each handler with a Swift-native body that calls the completion handler from Swift (.pointee(args)). This requires translating each method's logic into Swift, which is Phase 2/4 territory for most of them. webProcessConnectionCountForTesting is the existing example.

(3) is the right long-term answer; (1)/(2) would just churn the trampoline location.

Also worth tracking here: the remaining non-completion-handler swiftStubs that stay for unrelated reasons:
  - swiftStubUpdateCaptureOrigin: [RefWrap] for SecurityOriginData (IRGen crash on by-value)
  - swiftStubConsumeAudioComponentRegistrations: `using AuxiliaryProcess::consumeAudioComponentRegistrations` -- clang importer doesn't surface using-declarations.

These two need separate attention (or just live with them until the parent C++ goes away).

title: Future: extend WebCore modulemap for direct Swift/C++ interop, remove C trampolines
description:

Today, every WebCore static call from Swift in the GPU process goes through an extern "C" trampoline in GPUProcess.cpp (e.g. WebKitGPUProcessVP9SetShouldEnableVP9Decoder, WebKitGPUProcessSetShouldListenToVoiceActivity, the mock-media bridges). The trampolines exist because Swift's clang importer doesn't see most WebCore types -- WebCore.MockRealtimeMediaSourceCenter, WebCore.RealtimeMediaSourceCenter, WebCore.VP9TestingOverrides, etc. all show up as "type 'WebCore' has no member 'X'" when called from Swift directly. Verified empirically 2026-05-20.

Root cause: the WebCore module exposed to Swift is essentially empty.
- Source/WebCore/WebCore.modulemap is just `framework module WebCore [system] {}` -- no header listing.
- The build emits Source/WebCore/WebCore_Private.modulemap with just two headers (DiagnosticLoggingKeys.h, DiagnosticLoggingClient.h) -- everything else WebCore that Swift sees is leaking through transitive #include from headers in the WebKit Swift import chain (e.g. WebCore.IntDegrees, WebCore.ProcessIdentifier are reachable that way, but most of WebCore is not).
- Adding headers to GPUProcessSwiftUtilities.h pulls types into Swift's view but anything templated (e.g. Vector<MockMediaDevice>) still needs a hand-written using-alias because Swift's clang importer doesn't auto-name C++ template instances.

Why this matters:
Removing the C trampolines would simplify the GPU-process Swift code -- one fewer file per WebCore touchpoint -- and let Swift hold WebCore reference types directly. It would also let us call into WebCore types that are themselves Swift (Source/WebGPU/WebGPU/Buffer.swift et al) without round-tripping through C bridges.

Why this is hard:
- The WebCore modulemap is intentionally minimal; expanding it can pull in transitive #includes that don't compile under Swift's clang importer (Foundation classes, Cocoa types, autogen-emitted code). Each header added is a rabbit-hole.
- Swift's clang importer is sensitive to multi-base-class inheritance, certain template patterns, and address-only types (we already hit the IRGen crash on SecurityOriginData; ~/swift-gpu-compiler-crash/ has the repro). Expanding the visible surface will surface more of these.
- The same modulemap audit would have to repeat for WebKit headers that pull in WebCore -- many of them transitively expose problematic types.
- WebCore is shared with non-Swift consumers (UIProcess, NetworkProcess); changes have to keep them building.

Suggested phasing when this work is taken on:
1. Pick a single WebCore subsystem with active Swift use (e.g. WebGPU's existing Swift code in Source/WebGPU/WebGPU/) and audit which headers Swift would need to see.
2. Build a separate WebCore_GPU.modulemap (or similar) carrying just those headers, scoped to the GPU process's Swift compilation -- don't change the global modulemap until the pattern is proven.
3. Identify and fix per-header Swift importability issues (class layouts, template instantiations needing using-aliases, etc.) one at a time.
4. Migrate one or two C trampolines to direct Swift calls as proof.
5. Decide if the cost of expanding the modulemap is worth it. If yes, plan rollout to other GPU-process Swift sites. If no, document why and accept the C-trampoline pattern as permanent.

Outcome target: each WebCore static call currently going through a `WebKitGPUProcess<X>` extern "C" bridge becomes a direct `WebCore.X.method(args)` call from Swift. Reduces the surface of hand-written C++ shim code on the ON path.
